subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Can the Industry Fix Itself?
description: A 60-second lesson on Can the Industry Fix Itself?.

hook.text: The coffee industry knows it has a problem. Farmer poverty, climate change, and deforestation threaten its own future.

buildup.text: Major companies have pledged sustainability goals—carbon neutrality, farmer income support, and reforestation.

discovery.text: Progress is real but slow. Only 25% of coffee is currently produced under any sustainability certification.

twist.text: Some argue that consumers ultimately hold the power—by choosing to pay more for transparent, ethical coffee.

climax.text: The question isn't whether coffee can be sustainable. It's whether the change will come fast enough to matter.

punchline.text: The industry that runs on beans now runs against the clock.

quiz.question: What percentage of coffee is currently produced under sustainability certification?

details.summary: The coffee industry faces interconnected crises: farmer poverty, climate change, deforestation, and inequality. Solutions require higher farm-gate prices, climate adaptation investment, transparent supply chains, and willing consumers.
details.whyItMatters: Without structural reform, the coffee industry risks losing its farming base to poverty and its growing regions to climate change within a generation.
takeaways: Farmer poverty, climate change, and inequality are interconnected
Higher farm-gate prices are the most direct solution
Reform requires action from all parts of the supply chain

faq.question: What would a fair coffee industry look like?
faq.answer: Farmers would earn a living income above production costs. Supply chains would be transparent about pricing at every stage. Environmental costs would be internalized. Consumers would pay slightly more per cup but know their money reaches growers. Some models already demonstrate this is possible.

faq.question: What can individuals do to support better coffee?
faq.answer: Buy from roasters that publish their sourcing practices and prices paid to farmers. Choose certified or direct-trade coffee. Be willing to pay a bit more for quality. Support organizations working on farmer education, climate adaptation, and market access. Small choices at scale create change.
